title: Climbing Mount Everest
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, is the highest mountain on Earth. Its summit stands 8,849 metres above sea level, which is more than ten times the height of the tallest building in the world. The mountain is known as Sagarmatha in Nepali and Chomolungma in Tibetan, and it was named in English after Sir George Everest, a British surveyor, although he never saw it. For climbers, the mountain has been a challenge for more than a century, and for the people who live beneath it, it is a sacred place.

The first serious attempts to climb Everest were made by British expeditions in the 1920s. In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine disappeared near the summit, and nobody knows whether they reached it; Mallory's body was found in 1999, but the question remains open. The mountain was finally climbed on 29 May 1953 by Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa from Nepal. They spent only about fifteen minutes on the top, and Hillary later described the view as the most beautiful that he had ever seen.

Climbing Everest is not a single effort but a long process. Expeditions usually spend six to eight weeks on the mountain, and most of this time is used for acclimatisation, the gradual process by which the body adapts to the thin air. Climbers go up to a higher camp, sleep there, and return to a lower one, repeating the process several times. There are four camps above Base Camp, which stands at 5,364 metres, and the climbers reach the summit from the highest one, Camp Four, in a final push of fifteen hours or more.

The most important danger is the lack of oxygen. At the summit, the air pressure is about one third of that at sea level, so each breath contains only a third of the oxygen. Most climbers use bottled oxygen above 8,000 metres, a region known as the death zone, where the body cannot recover and grows weaker every hour. The cold is also severe, with temperatures as low as minus forty degrees Celsius, and the wind can exceed two hundred kilometres an hour, which makes any mistake extremely dangerous.

Sherpas, an ethnic group from the high valleys of Nepal, play a crucial part in every expedition. They carry equipment, fix ropes and set up camps, work that is both difficult and dangerous. The mountain has claimed more than three hundred lives since the first attempt, and about a third of the dead have been Sherpas. In recent years, Sherpas have campaigned for better pay and insurance, and some have become famous climbers in their own right, with record numbers of ascents to their names.

The popularity of Everest has created new problems. In some years, over eight hundred people have reached the summit, and queues have formed on the narrow ridge near the top, where climbers wait for hours in the cold. The mountain is also littered with discarded tents, bottles and oxygen cylinders, and human waste from the camps pollutes the glaciers. The Nepalese government now requires climbers to bring their waste back down, and teams of Sherpas have removed tonnes of rubbish.

Climate change is changing the mountain itself. The glaciers on which the route depends are melting faster, which makes the icefall at the start of the climb less stable. Dr Pema Lama, a glaciologist, says that some of the ice may disappear within a generation. She also notes that melting reveals bodies and equipment left decades ago. Even so, the number of people who wish to climb does not decline, and each year the debate about whether the mountain should be limited to fewer visitors becomes louder.
